subject: medicine
title: DVLA — the patient who won't stop driving
question: A doctor has told a patient that a recent diagnosis means they must inform the DVLA and stop driving. At the next appointment the patient says they have not told the DVLA and are still driving to work. What should the doctor be thinking about?
answer: Discussion question — no single verdict, but the sequence is real and published: explain the duty (which sits with the DRIVER, not the doctor), make every reasonable effort to persuade them to stop, assess whether continued driving risks death or serious harm to OTHERS, and only then — as a last resort — disclose to the DVLA, telling the patient beforehand where practicable and confirming in writing afterwards.
modelReasoningPath: A strong candidate does not jump straight to 'report them'. They first note the legal duty to notify sits with the driver, not the doctor — the doctor's job is to explain that duty and try to persuade. They ask WHY the patient is still driving (work, independence, caring responsibilities) rather than treating refusal as obstinacy. Only then do they apply a threshold: does continued driving expose OTHERS to a risk of death or serious harm? If so, disclosure to the DVLA is a last resort, done in a way that tells the patient first if practicable and confirms in writing afterwards. Confidentiality is a default being carefully departed from, not a rule with an exception bolted on.

rubric.strong: States the legal duty sits with the driver, describes persuasion before disclosure, applies a risk-to-others threshold, treats disclosure as a last-resort balance (not automatic), and mentions telling the patient beforehand and confirming in writing afterwards.
rubric.developing: Reaches the right end point but skips a step in the sequence — usually the persuasion step or the risk-to-others threshold — or is vague about when disclosure becomes justified.
rubric.weak: Says the doctor must report the patient to the DVLA as the doctor's own legal duty, or says confidentiality is absolute and nothing can be done, with no risk reasoning either way.

commonMistakes.mistake: States the doctor has a legal duty to report the patient
commonMistakes.reveals: This is the single most widely-taught error in this area — the DRIVER carries the legal duty; the doctor's duty is to explain it and try to persuade

commonMistakes.mistake: Jumps straight to disclosure with no persuasion or risk assessment
commonMistakes.reveals: Skips the professional sequence — persuade first, assess risk to others, warn, then disclose

commonMistakes.mistake: Says confidentiality is absolute and nothing can be done
commonMistakes.reveals: Confidentiality is a strong default, not an absolute rule — GMC guidance permits disclosure where others face risk of death or serious harm

liveProbes.probe: What would you want to understand about why they're still driving before doing anything else?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Names a plausible reason (work, caring responsibilities, independence) rather than assuming obstinacy

liveProbes.probe: Does it matter whether they drive alone to work, or drive a school minibus?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Recognises the risk-to-others threshold scales with who else is exposed

hints: Whose legal duty is it to tell the DVLA — the doctor's, or the patient's?
What would the doctor try before ever considering breaking confidentiality?
What threshold would justify overriding the patient's confidentiality here?

subject: medicine
title: Two weeks later, nothing has happened
question: You raised a concern with your supervisor two weeks ago about something you thought was unsafe. As far as you can tell, nothing has changed. What do you do now?
answer: Discussion question — no single verdict. A strong answer treats silence as information, not resolution: names a specific next step (check what happened to the concern, ask directly, escalate to whoever is above the original person if there's still no answer), and does not simply let it drop because the first attempt was made in good faith.
modelReasoningPath: This station exists because 'I'd tell someone senior' is treated as a complete answer across the market when it is only the first half. A strong candidate recognises that raising a concern once and hearing nothing is not the same as the concern being addressed. They ask what happened to it directly, rather than assuming silence means it was dealt with or that raising it again would be pushy. If there's still no answer, they escalate — to whoever is next up the chain, or to a different channel entirely if the original person is unresponsive or part of the problem. They do this without treating it as a personal grudge against the first person.

rubric.strong: Does not accept silence as resolution, follows up directly and specifically on what happened, and names a genuine next step if there's still no answer — including who that next step goes to.
rubric.developing: Says they would 'check in' or 'follow up' but is vague about with whom, or on what timescale, or what they'd do if that also went nowhere.
rubric.weak: Assumes it must have been dealt with because nothing more has been said, or does nothing further because they already raised it once.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assumes silence means the concern was resolved
commonMistakes.reveals: Confuses the absence of news with good news — a candidate needs to check, not assume

commonMistakes.mistake: Says 'I'd leave it, I already did my bit'
commonMistakes.reveals: Treats raising a concern once as discharging responsibility for it, rather than following it through

liveProbes.probe: Who, specifically, would you go to next?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Names an actual role or route (someone above the original person, a different channel), not just 'someone else'

liveProbes.probe: What if that person is also unresponsive?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Has a further step in mind rather than running out of options after the second attempt

hints: Does silence tell you the concern was addressed, or just that nothing visible has changed?
What would you actually say if you followed up on it directly?
If following up again didn't work, who else could you go to?

subject: medicine
title: A capacitous adult refuses help
question: An older man living alone refuses all offers of help, even though his home is in a poor state and he has had a couple of falls. He understands the risks and is clear he wants to be left to make his own choices. His daughter is desperate for someone to intervene. What do you think should happen?
answer: Discussion question — no single verdict. A strong answer holds the line that a person able to understand, weigh and communicate a decision has the right to make an unwise one, and does not let genuine distress from a third party (the daughter) override that — while still taking her concern seriously and looking for what CAN legitimately be offered.
modelReasoningPath: The station is built around the principle that a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because it is unwise — and this is exactly the principle candidates abandon first under pressure, especially when a sympathetic relative is pushing hard. A strong candidate holds the line: if he understands the risks and can communicate his choice, his autonomy stands, however uncomfortable that is to watch. They do not conclude he 'must' lack capacity because the decision seems irrational to an outsider. They also don't dismiss the daughter — they look for what remains legitimately on offer (checking in, leaving the door open for him to accept help later, addressing immediate specific risks he might not object to) without overriding his stated choice.

rubric.strong: States clearly that an unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity, holds this position under the pressure of the daughter's distress, and still finds a genuine, non-overriding way to keep supporting him and take her concern seriously.
rubric.developing: States the principle but wobbles on whether it should really apply here, or resolves the tension by quietly deciding he probably lacks capacity because the decision seems extreme.
rubric.weak: Concludes he should be made to accept help because it's for his own good, or because his daughter is so worried, with no engagement with what capacity actually means.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assumes he must lack capacity because the decision seems irrational
commonMistakes.reveals: The most common capacity error — capacity is about the ability to understand and weigh a decision, not about agreeing with the outcome

commonMistakes.mistake: Concludes his daughter's distress should tip the balance toward intervening anyway
commonMistakes.reveals: Confuses a third party's discomfort with a reason to override the person's own autonomous choice

liveProbes.probe: What if his falls get worse — does that change your answer?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Distinguishes between reassessing capacity if something genuinely changes and simply escalating pressure because the outcome is feared

liveProbes.probe: Is there anything that could legitimately be done here without overriding him?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Names something concrete — checking in regularly, addressing one specific hazard he doesn't object to — rather than 'nothing' or 'force help on him'

hints: Does making an unwise decision mean someone lacks the capacity to make it?
What is actually being asked for here — is it about the risk, or about someone else's distress at the risk?
What could still be offered without overriding his own choice?

subject: medicine
title: The under-16 who doesn't want her parents told
question: A 15-year-old comes to see a doctor alone and asks about contraception. She says she doesn't want her parents to know. What is the doctor thinking about here?
answer: Discussion question — no single verdict, though this draws on a real UK framework: Gillick competence (is this specific young person able to understand and weigh THIS decision?) and, distinct from it, the Fraser criteria (the narrower test specific to contraception and sexual health advice). A strong answer keeps these two separate rather than treating them as interchangeable, and weighs her right to confidential healthcare against any signs that would raise a safeguarding concern (a much older partner, signs of coercion).
modelReasoningPath: This is a deliberate correction station: candidates are very commonly taught Fraser as if it were the general test of a child's competence, when Gillick is the general test and Fraser is specific to contraception and sexual health. A strong candidate keeps the two separate — she may be Gillick competent in general, but the Fraser criteria (would she be likely to have sex anyway, would her health suffer without advice, is it in her best interests) are the specific gate for THIS kind of advice. They also recognise that even where these are met, safeguarding is not overridden by competence: if something suggests coercion or a much older partner, that changes the picture regardless of her competence. A candidate who reaches for Gillick without ever reaching for safeguarding has only half-answered.

rubric.strong: Distinguishes Gillick (general competence) from Fraser (contraception-specific), recognises confidentiality is a strong default that depends on assessing competence, and independently raises safeguarding as a separate consideration that isn't overridden by competence.
rubric.developing: Reaches for one of the two frameworks reasonably but conflates it with the other, or discusses confidentiality without raising safeguarding at all.
rubric.weak: States a flat rule ('under 16s can't consent without parents' or 'it's entirely her choice, no exceptions') with no engagement with competence or safeguarding.

commonMistakes.mistake: Uses 'Fraser guidelines' as the general test of whether she can make decisions
commonMistakes.reveals: The most common error in this space — Fraser is specific to contraception/sexual health; Gillick is the general competence test

commonMistakes.mistake: Treats her stated confidentiality wish as settling the matter with no safeguarding check
commonMistakes.reveals: Confidentiality and safeguarding are separate questions — competence to consent doesn't remove the need to check for coercion

liveProbes.probe: What if she mentioned her partner was significantly older?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Recognises this shifts the situation toward a safeguarding concern regardless of her stated competence

liveProbes.probe: Is Gillick competence the same thing as meeting the Fraser criteria?
liveProbes.goodResponse: States clearly that they are not the same test and explains the difference

hints: Is there a difference between asking 'can she understand this decision' and 'should contraceptive advice specifically be given without her parents knowing'?
What would make you more concerned about this situation, beyond her age alone?
Does her being able to consent mean there's nothing else to think about here?

subject: medicine
title: Your supervisor asks you to do something you think is wrong
question: Someone senior to you asks you to do something as part of a task you're helping with, and you think it's the wrong thing to do. What do you consider?
answer: Discussion question — no single verdict. A strong answer neither simply complies nor simply refuses: it names a way to raise the concern respectfully in the moment (a question rather than an accusation), proposes an alternative where possible, and is honest about what they'd do if the concern isn't resolved — without assuming bad faith on the senior person's part.
modelReasoningPath: A strong candidate resists the binary of 'comply' or 'refuse and walk away'. They first assume good faith — the senior person may have information or a reason the candidate doesn't have — and raise it as a genuine question rather than an accusation: 'can I check why we're doing it this way?' If the concern isn't resolved, they look for a workable alternative rather than only objecting. They are honest, without being confrontational, about what they would do if asked to go ahead regardless — which might mean declining that specific part while still being constructive about the rest of the task. The seniority gap doesn't remove the need to speak up; it changes HOW you do it, not WHETHER you do it.

rubric.strong: Neither complies unquestioningly nor refuses outright; raises the concern as a genuine question, proposes something workable, and is honest about their own limit if the concern isn't addressed — without threatening or lecturing.
rubric.developing: Says they would raise a concern but is vague about how, or defaults to either full compliance or a flat refusal without trying a middle path.
rubric.weak: Complies without comment because the person is senior, or refuses and escalates immediately with no attempt to understand or resolve it directly first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Complies because the person is senior, with no further thought
commonMistakes.reveals: Prioritises deference over judgement — a real professionalism red flag

commonMistakes.mistake: Refuses and immediately threatens to report it
commonMistakes.reveals: Skips the respectful, direct conversation that should come first in most cases

liveProbes.probe: What if they brushed off your question and told you to just get on with it?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Names a further step (raising it with someone else, or declining that specific part) rather than complying anyway

liveProbes.probe: Does it matter if you might be missing some context they have?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Acknowledges this is genuinely possible and frames the challenge as a question, not an accusation

hints: Is the choice really just between doing what you're told and refusing outright?
How could you raise this as a question rather than an accusation?
What would you actually do if raising it didn't change anything?

subject: medicine
title: A colleague makes a remark about a resident's family
question: A colleague you respect and who has worked somewhere for years makes a dismissive, generalising remark about a resident's family while you're both on a break. What do you do?
answer: Discussion question — no single verdict. A strong answer says something in the moment rather than only reporting it afterwards, addresses the specific phrase rather than labelling the person's character, and doesn't let the seniority or likeability of the colleague stop them from responding.
modelReasoningPath: This station tests whether a candidate can respond to a discriminatory remark from someone they like and who has more experience than them — the hardest version of this problem, and the one most candidates avoid by staying quiet and reporting it later, if at all. A strong candidate says something in the room, addressing the specific words used rather than accusing the person of being a bad person, which keeps the conversation open rather than triggering pure defensiveness. They don't accept it with a laugh or let it pass in silence. If it turns out to be part of a pattern, or has happened in front of the people being talked about, they recognise this needs to go further than a private word.

rubric.strong: Says something in the moment, addresses the specific remark rather than the person's character, doesn't defer to seniority or friendliness, and recognises when it needs to be escalated beyond a private conversation.
rubric.developing: Would raise it eventually but only after the moment has passed, or is vague about what they'd actually say in the room.
rubric.weak: Says nothing because the person is respected or senior, or laughs along to avoid an awkward moment.

commonMistakes.mistake: Says nothing in the moment, planning to 'mention it later' vaguely
commonMistakes.reveals: Avoiding the immediate, harder conversation in favour of a safer, deferred one that may never happen

commonMistakes.mistake: Accuses the colleague of being a bad person rather than naming the remark
commonMistakes.reveals: Makes the conversation about character rather than behaviour, which usually shuts it down rather than opening it

liveProbes.probe: What would you actually say, in the moment, without it turning into a confrontation?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Offers a specific, low-heat form of words that names the phrase rather than the person

liveProbes.probe: Does it matter that you get on well with this person?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Recognises the temptation to let it go because of the relationship, and says why that shouldn't change the response

hints: Is it easier, but worse, to say nothing and mention it 'later'?
How could you name the specific words rather than the person's character?
Would your answer change if this had happened in front of the family being talked about?

subject: medicine
title: Should a smoker wait longer for surgery?
question: Someone suggests that patients who smoke should wait longer for planned surgery than patients who don't, since smoking increases their own surgical risk and worsens outcomes. What do you think of that argument?
answer: Discussion question — no single verdict. A strong answer engages seriously with both the clinical-risk argument (smoking genuinely affects surgical outcomes) and the desert-based objection (using a lifestyle factor to ration care risks penalising ill health rather than treating it, and could apply inconsistently to many other lifestyle factors), without dismissing either side.
modelReasoningPath: A strong candidate separates two different arguments that often get run together: a CLINICAL argument (smoking affects wound healing and surgical risk, so a delay to optimise a patient — e.g. supported smoking cessation before surgery — may genuinely improve their outcome) from a DESERT-based argument (smokers 'deserve' to wait longer because their condition is self-inflicted). They can support the first while being wary of the second, noting that a consistent desert-based approach would need to apply to many other lifestyle-linked conditions (diet, alcohol, inactivity), which most people find uncomfortable once stated plainly. This mirrors the same reasoning used for other 'self-caused' illness debates and rewards spotting that pattern.

rubric.strong: Separates the clinical-optimisation justification from the moral-desert justification, engages with why a consistent desert-based approach would need to apply far more broadly, and reaches a considered rather than reflexive position.
rubric.developing: Takes a position but doesn't distinguish the clinical case from the moral case, treating them as the same argument.
rubric.weak: States smokers 'brought it on themselves' with no engagement with clinical justification or the fairness objection, or insists lifestyle should never be relevant with no engagement with genuine clinical risk.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treats a genuine clinical-optimisation reason and a moral-blame reason as the same argument
commonMistakes.reveals: Hasn't separated 'this affects the medical outcome' from 'this person deserves to wait' — very different justifications that happen to point the same way

commonMistakes.mistake: Says lifestyle should never be considered at all
commonMistakes.reveals: Ignores that clinical optimisation before surgery (e.g. supported cessation) is a genuinely different, more defensible idea than punishment

liveProbes.probe: Would the same logic apply to someone needing surgery after a diet-related condition, or a sports injury?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Recognises the logic would need to generalise, and engages with how uncomfortable that generalisation is

liveProbes.probe: Is there a version of 'wait longer' that's actually about improving the outcome rather than punishing the patient?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Names supported smoking cessation or pre-surgical optimisation as a distinct, defensible idea

hints: Is 'this affects your surgical outcome' the same argument as 'you deserve to wait'?
Would the same logic have to apply to other lifestyle-linked conditions?
Is there a version of a delay that's about improving the outcome rather than blame?

subject: medicine
title: Which two principles are actually in conflict here?
question: A patient with capacity refuses a treatment her family believes she needs, and the family is asking the team to override her. Talk me through the ethical tension here — and be specific about what's actually in conflict.
answer: Discussion question — no single verdict. This station is purpose-built to score ZERO for simply naming the four principles of biomedical ethics (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice) and full marks for identifying WHICH TWO are actually in tension here (autonomy versus beneficence, most directly) and what would make one give way.
modelReasoningPath: Reciting 'autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice' answers a different, easier question than the one asked. A strong candidate goes straight past the list and names the specific tension: the patient's right to decide for herself (autonomy) versus the clinical team and family's wish to act in what they see as her best interest (beneficence). They explain why autonomy generally wins where capacity is present — a patient does not have to justify her reasons to anyone — while being honest that this is genuinely uncomfortable to watch, not a clean win. A very strong candidate notices that non-maleficence and justice aren't really live tensions in this specific scenario at all, which is itself evidence they're reasoning about THIS case rather than reciting a memorised list.

rubric.strong: Does not just name the four principles; identifies specifically that autonomy and beneficence are in tension here, explains why autonomy generally prevails given capacity, and is honest about what remains uncomfortable about that outcome.
rubric.developing: Names the four principles and gestures at 'a conflict between them' without saying specifically which two, or applies the tension only loosely to this case.
rubric.weak: Recites the four principles as if naming them answers the question, with no application to this specific scenario — this scores ZERO on the reasoning dimension regardless of how fluently they're listed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Names all four principles and stops there
commonMistakes.reveals: This is the exact behaviour the station is built to catch — naming the framework is not the same as using it, and scores nothing on its own

commonMistakes.mistake: Says all four principles are equally in conflict
commonMistakes.reveals: Hasn't actually identified which two are doing the real work in this specific scenario

liveProbes.probe: You named the four principles — which two are actually pulling against each other HERE?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Names autonomy and beneficence specifically, not a restated list

liveProbes.probe: What would have to be true for the family's view to win instead?
liveProbes.goodResponse: Engages with a concrete condition — e.g. doubt about her capacity — rather than refusing to imagine it

hints: Naming a list of principles isn't the same as identifying a conflict — which two are actually pulling against each other here?
Why does autonomy usually win when a patient has capacity?
What would have to change for the answer to go the other way?
